questions.q: Clinical psychology is the practical aspect of
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Clinical psychology applies the theory and findings of abnormal psychology to the assessment and treatment of psychological disorders.

questions.q: One of the reasons to study psychology is
options: to learn how to manipulate others.
to have the answers to all of life's questions.
to completely understand and predict human behavior.
to understand the human mind and how it works.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. A core, legitimate reason to study psychology is to better understand the human mind and how it works — the other options overstate or misrepresent psychology's goals.

questions.q: The "father" of psychology and founder of the first psychological laboratory was
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Wilhelm Wundt founded the first psychology laboratory in Leipzig in 1879, earning him the title 'father of psychology'.

questions.q: Edward Titchener's school of thought, focused on the structure of the mind, is known as:
questions.explain: Titchener developed structuralism in the US (1892), focused on breaking down the structure of the mind using introspection.

questions.q: You see a psychologist and tell her that you are feeling depressed. The psychologist talks to you about your past and attempts to link your present situation with patterns developed in your childhood during your relationship with your parents. The psychologist would probably belong to which school of psychology?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Linking current issues to unresolved childhood conflicts and early relationships with parents is characteristic of the psychodynamic approach.

questions.q: J.B. Watson, the founder and father of the behaviouristic school of psychology, defines psychology as the science of ...
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Watson founded behaviourism specifically to redefine psychology as the science of observable behaviour, rejecting the study of the unobservable mind or consciousness.

questions.q: The philosophical debate over whether behaviour results from free choice or from observable, measurable causes is called:
questions.explain: Free will versus determinism asks whether behaviour is a result of independent decisions or of measurable, deterministic causes.

questions.q: The structuralist school of psychology
options: used introspection to analyze conscious experience.
used dream analysis to reveal the unconscious.
relied heavily on the concept of natural selection.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Structuralism used introspection — trained self-report of conscious experience — to analyse the basic structure of the mind.

questions.q: __________ psychology is associated with emotions, planning, critical thinking and learning.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Cognitive psychology studies mental processes including thinking, planning, learning, and (in applied contexts) their links to emotion.

questions.q: Psychodynamic psychology differs from other approaches because it is based on
options: thoughts and impulses outside of conscious experience.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Psychodynamic psychology is distinguished by its focus on unconscious thoughts and impulses, outside of conscious awareness.

questions.q: A pseudo-psychology that claims personality traits can be read from the shape of the skull is:
questions.explain: Phrenology claims personality traits are revealed by the shape of the skull; it is not scientifically supported.

questions.q: "Experience cannot be analyzed successfully into its elements" would likely be said by a
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. This directly reflects the Gestalt principle that experience must be understood as an organized whole, not broken into separate elements.

questions.q: Which approach to psychology was Edward Titchener associated with in the 1800s?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Edward Titchener brought Wundt's ideas to the US and founded structuralism, focused on analysing the structure of conscious experience.

questions.q: Which major paradigm in psychology focuses on unconscious motives and conflicts (id, ego, superego) as determinants of behaviour?
questions.explain: The psychoanalytic paradigm, founded by Freud, focuses on unconscious motives and conflicts, using concepts like the id, ego, and superego.

questions.q: Which paradigm emphasizes self-directed behaviour, personal growth, and each person's unique potential?
questions.explain: Humanism, associated with Maslow, Rogers, and May, emphasizes personal growth, self-concept, and reaching one's full potential.

questions.q: In the scientific method, a tentative explanation of an event or relationship — an educated guess about behaviour — is called a:
questions.explain: A hypothesis is a tentative, testable explanation or educated guess about a behaviour or relationship.

questions.q: You volunteer for a psychology experiment where the experimenter rings a bell and shoots a puff of air into your eyes, making you blink. After a few trials, you blink as soon as you hear the bell alone. In this example, the bell is the ______, and the puff of air is the ______.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. The bell, originally neutral, becomes the conditioned stimulus (CS) once paired with the puff of air. The puff of air naturally and automatically triggers blinking without any learning, making it the unconditioned stimulus (US).

questions.q: A study in which neither the participants nor the observer know who received the real treatment is called a:
questions.explain: In a double-blind study, both the observer and participants are unaware of who is in the treatment vs. control group, reducing bias.

questions.q: Improvement due to the mere expectation of receiving treatment, rather than the treatment itself, is called the:
questions.explain: The placebo effect is improvement that occurs because of the expectation of getting better from treatment, even without an active treatment.

questions.q: Psychology is considered a science because it
options: gains information through new methods and technology.
accepts what seems plausible and sensible.
studies animal as well as human behavior.
relies on direct observation and measurement of behavior.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Psychology qualifies as a science because it relies on direct, systematic observation and measurement, not merely plausibility or intuition.

questions.q: Changes in a subject's behaviour caused by their awareness of being observed is called:
questions.explain: The observer effect refers to changes in behaviour caused specifically by the subject's awareness that they are being watched.

questions.q: A correlation coefficient of -0.75 compared to +0.25 indicates:
questions.explain: The strength of a correlation is shown by the absolute value of the coefficient, not its sign — |-0.75| = 0.75 is stronger than |+0.25| = 0.25.

questions.q: Psychology is the science and study of
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Psychology studies the behaviour and mental processes of living organisms broadly — including both humans and animals — not humans alone.

questions.q: Which ethical consideration in research refers to participants freely choosing to take part without coercion?
questions.explain: Voluntary participation means individuals choose to take part in research of their own free will, without coercion.

questions.q: The study of similarities and differences in the behavior of different species is called
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Comparative psychology specifically studies similarities and differences in behaviour across different animal species.

questions.q: Which ancient philosopher proposed a tripartite hierarchical division of the psyche into the rational, spirited/affective, and appetitive?
questions.explain: Plato proposed a tripartite hierarchical division of the psyche: the rational, the spirited/affective, and the appetitive.

questions.q: Which of the following psychological theories is known as the one that emphasizes "free will"?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Humanistic psychology, rooted in existentialist thought, emphasizes free will and personal choice, unlike the deterministic views of psychodynamic and behaviourist theories.

questions.q: Wilhelm Wundt's research focus included sensory physiology, conscious experiences, and:
questions.explain: Wundt's focus included sensory physiology, conscious experiences, and cultural differences in behaviour (motivation, voluntary control, cognitive processes).

questions.q: The goals of psychology are to
options: compare, analyze, and control human behavior.
explain the functioning of the human mind.
describe, predict, understand, and control behavior.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. The four standard goals of psychology are to describe, explain/understand, predict, and control behaviour.

questions.q: Galton's work on human intelligence testing was influenced by whose theory?
questions.explain: Galton's human intelligence testing (1869) was influenced by Charles Darwin's theory of natural selection.

questions.q: Psychology is
options: the study of human origins, evolution, and cultures.
the scientific study of behavior and mental processes of any living creature.
a natural science integrating physiology and neurology.
the deductive study of forms and functions of human groups.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. The standard definition of psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes.

questions.q: Behaviorism helped make psychology a
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. By insisting on studying only observable, measurable behaviour, behaviourism helped establish psychology as a rigorous science.

questions.q: Which specialization focuses on changes in behaviour over a person's age/lifespan?
questions.explain: Developmental psychologists study changes in behaviour over age.

questions.q: Psychology at the workplace is...
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Industrial and organizational (I/O) psychology is the specialization focused on human behaviour in workplace settings.

questions.q: Of the following, who is associated with the Gestalt school of psychology?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Max Wertheimer is a founding figure of Gestalt psychology, famous for studying perceived motion (the phi phenomenon).

questions.q: The process by which a trained psychologist uses knowledge obtained from psychology to help people solve psychological problems is called...
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Psychotherapy is the general term for the practical application of psychological knowledge to help people address psychological problems. Psychoanalysis is one specific type of therapy; psychiatry is a medical specialty.

questions.q: Graphology is the false claim that personality traits can be revealed through:
questions.explain: Graphology falsely claims that personality traits are revealed by a person's handwriting.

questions.q: Telepathy, as defined in parapsychology, refers to:
options: Ability of mind over matter without any known medium
Knowledge of hidden objects outside physical reach
Communication between two minds without known sensory channels
questions.explain: Telepathy is communication between two minds without the use of known sensory channels.

questions.q: Clairvoyance, as defined in parapsychology, refers to:
options: Knowledge of hidden objects or events outside physical reach
questions.explain: Clairvoyance is knowledge of hidden objects or events occurring outside the physical reach of the person.

questions.q: Psychokinesis (PK) is best described as:
options: Rebirth of a non-physical aspect of consciousness
The ability of the mind over matter, time, space, or energy without a known medium
questions.explain: Psychokinesis is the ability of the mind to influence matter, time, space, or energy without any known medium.

questions.q: You see a psychologist and tell her that you are feeling depressed. She talks to you about the goals you have for yourself, about your image of yourself, and about the choices that you make in your life and that you could make in your life. This psychologist would probably belong to the __________ school of psychology.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Focusing on personal goals, self-image, and free choice reflects the humanistic school of psychology.

questions.q: Some topics in psychology are difficult to study because
options: they overlap with other fields, such as law and business.
of a lack of interest in human behavior.
advanced technology that measures brain waves is not available.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Ethical considerations (e.g. the inability to ethically manipulate certain variables in humans) limit what psychologists can directly study.

questions.q: According to John B. Watson, psychology is the study of
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Watson redefined psychology as the study of observable behaviour, rejecting the study of the mind/consciousness as unscientific.

questions.q: Which growing field in recent trends in psychology focuses specifically on the nervous system and brain activity?
questions.explain: Neuroscience, a growing field in recent psychology trends, focuses on the nervous system and brain activity.

questions.q: In the scientific method's application example, Suzanne's initial observation was that some managers seem to experience:
questions.explain: Suzanne observed that some business managers seem to experience less work-related stress than others.

questions.q: In Suzanne's experiment on stress, the group allowed to set their own pace (versus a forced pace) reported:
questions.explain: The self-paced group reported lower stress levels than the forced-pace group, supporting Suzanne's hypothesis that control over tasks reduces stress.

questions.q: A theory, as described in the scientific method, can be best defined as:
options: A tentative explanation of events that can be disproven by new evidence
The final step of the scientific method with no further questioning possible
questions.explain: Theories are tentative explanations of events or occurrences, and can be disproven in the face of new evidence.

questions.q: According to the cholesterol theory example, excess cholesterol deposited in artery walls can lead to heart disease by:
options: Narrowing artery diameter and causing tissue damage when blood flow is blocked
questions.explain: The cholesterol theory holds that excess cholesterol deposits narrow artery diameter, causing tissue damage if blood flow becomes blocked.

questions.q: Who was the father of Experimental Psychology?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Wilhelm Wundt founded the first experimental psychology laboratory in Leipzig, Germany, in 1879, earning him the title 'father of experimental psychology'.

questions.q: To control for external variables in an experiment, researchers use randomization and:
questions.explain: Researchers control external variables through randomization and by holding other variables constant.

questions.q: The group in an experiment that is exposed to the treatment (independent variable) is called the:
questions.explain: The experimental group is the group exposed to the treatment (the independent variable) in an experiment.

questions.q: An inactive pill or treatment with no known active effects is called a:
questions.explain: A placebo is an inactive pill or treatment that has no known active effects.

questions.q: The study of mental processes such as thinking, perception, information processing, etc. is a key element in __________ psychology.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Cognitive psychology is defined by its focus on mental processes such as thinking, perception, and information processing.

questions.q: Which is a disadvantage of the experimental method noted in the lecture?
options: It never requires a control group
It is the only method that can be used in psychology
It is sometimes not feasible or ethical to manipulate certain variables
questions.explain: A disadvantage of experiments is that they are sometimes not feasible, may not generalize to other contexts, and are sometimes not ethical to conduct (manipulating certain variables).

questions.q: Descriptive methods in non-experimental research include observational techniques, case studies, and:
questions.explain: Descriptive methods include observational techniques, case studies, and survey research — providing objective, detailed descriptions of behaviour.

questions.q: Which area in psychology would be most likely to study the phenomenon of "peer influence"?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Social psychology studies how people are influenced by others, including peer influence and group dynamics.

questions.q: In survey research, subtle changes in the order or wording of a question can produce major effects — this is called:
questions.explain: Wording effects describe how even subtle changes in question order or wording can significantly affect survey responses.

questions.q: In survey research terminology, the entire group of people that a researcher is studying is called the:
questions.explain: The population is the entire group of people that a researcher is studying, while the sample is the subset that actually participates.

questions.q: A sampling technique ensuring every individual in a population has an equal chance of being selected is called:
questions.explain: Random sampling obtains a representative sample by ensuring each individual in the population has an equal opportunity to be included.

questions.q: The eclectic approach
options: embraces a variety of theoretical views.
has disappeared entirely as a perspective in psychology.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. The eclectic approach draws from and embraces multiple theoretical perspectives rather than committing to just one.

questions.q: The belief that all behaviour originates from childhood experiences residing in the unconscious is called:
questions.explain: Psychic determinism is the belief that all behaviour originates from unconscious childhood experiences.

questions.q: In Freud's topography of mind, the part containing information that is very hard or impossible to consciously retrieve is the:
questions.explain: The unconscious contains information that the individual is not aware of and that is hard or impossible to retrieve.

questions.q: In Freud's structural model, which part operates on the 'pleasure principle', driving immediate satisfaction?
questions.explain: The id contains innate sexual and aggressive instincts and operates on the pleasure principle, seeking immediate satisfaction.

questions.q: Which part of Freud's structural model operates on the 'reality principle', mediating between innate desires and moral standards?
questions.explain: The ego mediates between the id's desires and the superego's moral standards, operating on the reality principle.

questions.q: Eclectic psychologists are known for
options: drawing on a variety of theoretical views.
stressing the role of the unconscious.
prescribing drugs to treat emotional disorders.
studying the brain and nervous system.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. By definition, eclectic psychologists draw on a variety of theoretical perspectives rather than sticking to one school.

questions.q: Getting rid of one's own undesirable characteristics by attributing them to others is the defense mechanism of:
questions.explain: Projection involves attributing one's own undesirable characteristics to other people.

questions.q: During times of stress, retreating to behaviours characteristic of an earlier developmental stage is called:
questions.explain: Regression involves retreating to comforting behaviours characteristic of an earlier stage of development during stress.

questions.q: The psychodynamic view emphasizes the role of __________ in development.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. The psychodynamic view centers on internal impulses, desires, and unconscious conflicts as the drivers of development and behaviour.

questions.q: A psychologist whose viewpoint is psychodynamic
options: focuses on self-image and self-actualization to explain behavior.
is usually eclectic in his practice.
emphasizes the study of observable behavior.
believes behavior is directed by forces within one's personality which are often unconscious.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. The psychodynamic viewpoint holds that behaviour is directed by often-unconscious forces within the personality.

questions.q: According to behaviourism, all behaviour is:
questions.explain: Behaviourists (Watson, Pavlov, Skinner, Thorndike) argue all behaviour is learnt from the environment, to the neglect of innate/inherited factors.

questions.q: A stimulus that naturally evokes an unlearned, reflexive response is called the:
questions.explain: The unconditioned stimulus (UCS) naturally and automatically triggers an unlearned reflexive response (the UCR), without any prior learning.

questions.q: The tendency for a conditioned response to occur, in weaker form, to stimuli similar to but different from the original conditioned stimulus is called:
questions.explain: Stimulus generalization is the tendency of a conditioned response to occur, in weaker form, in response to similar (but not identical) stimuli.

questions.q: Thorndike's law of effect states that behaviours leading to reward tend to:
questions.explain: The law of effect states that behaviours leading to reward increase in strength, while those leading to punishment decrease in strength.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes Maslow's concept of self-actualization?
options: the need to develop one's potential fully
the need to feel a part of a higher spiritual order
the need to protect one's self-image through self-deception
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Self-actualization, per Maslow, is the need to fully develop and realize one's own unique potential.

questions.q: Of the following, who is a humanistic psychologist?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Abraham Maslow, known for the hierarchy of needs and self-actualization, is a founding humanistic psychologist.

questions.q: According to the __________ view, the need for love, self-esteem, belonging, self expression, and creativity are as important as biological needs.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. The humanistic view (e.g. Maslow's hierarchy) holds that psychological needs like love, esteem, and self-expression are just as important as basic biological needs.

questions.q: According to Rogers' person-centered approach, psychological distress is most likely when:
options: The self-concept closely matches the ideal self
There is little match between self-concept and ideal self
A person receives unconditional positive regard
questions.explain: Rogers suggested that a large mismatch between a person's self-concept and their ideal self leads to psychological distress; a close match leads to high self-esteem.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of Rogers' core conditions necessary for therapeutic change?
questions.explain: Rogers' three core conditions are empathy, unconditional positive regard, and congruence/genuineness — reinforcement is a behaviourist, not humanistic, concept.

questions.q: Cognitive theories view the mind as analogous to a(n):
questions.explain: Cognitive theories view the mind as an information processor, computing answers to problems similarly to a computer.

questions.q: A cognitive structure containing knowledge about a thing, its attributes, and relations among attributes is called a:
questions.explain: A schema is a cognitive structure containing organized knowledge about a concept, guiding perception and interpretation.

questions.q: A series of responses that gradually approach a desired pattern of behavior are called
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Successive approximations are the small steps gradually shaped toward a final target behaviour, the basis of the shaping procedure.

questions.q: The biopsychosocial(s) model explains behaviour by focusing on:
questions.explain: The biopsychosocial(s) model considers biological, psychological, and social factors — with consideration of a spiritual component — in explaining behaviour.

questions.q: Freud began experimenting with hypnosis after becoming interested in how the 'mind' could influence:
questions.explain: Freud was interested in how the mind could influence physical symptoms of the body, leading him to experiment with hypnosis.

questions.q: Freud collaborated with which colleague in developing the idea that neuroses originate in forgotten childhood trauma?
questions.explain: In collaboration with his friend Josef Breuer, Freud developed the idea that many neuroses had origins in forgotten childhood trauma.

questions.q: According to psychoanalytic theory, behaviour is explained through an interaction between innate drives and:
questions.explain: Behaviour is explained as an interaction between innate drives (those we are born with) and early experiences in childhood.

questions.q: Which part of Freud's topography of mind deals with the 'here and now'?
questions.explain: The conscious mind deals with the here and now, in contrast to the pre-conscious and unconscious.

questions.q: Repression refers to
options: thoughts mistakenly held out of awareness.
thoughts actively held out of awareness.
the fact that all thoughts, emotions, and actions are determined.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Repression, a Freudian defense mechanism, is the active (though unconscious) exclusion of anxiety-provoking thoughts from awareness.

questions.q: The kind of therapy developed by Freud is called
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Freud developed psychoanalysis, a therapy aimed at uncovering unconscious conflicts through techniques like free association.

questions.q: Frequent conflicts among the id, ego, and superego cause the individual to experience:
questions.explain: Frequent conflicts among the id, ego, and superego cause the individual to experience anxiety.

questions.q: Defense mechanisms are strategies designed to protect the individual against painful anxiety and ensure that:
questions.explain: Defense mechanisms protect against painful anxiety and ensure the ego is not overwhelmed by conflict.

questions.q: Comparative psychologists are primarily interested in
options: the comparison of different types of psychotherapy.
the comparison of functional and behavioral psychology.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Comparative psychology studies and compares the behaviour of different animal species, often to understand principles applicable to humans.

questions.q: When an anxiety-laden impulse, thought, or feeling is replaced in consciousness by its opposite, this defense mechanism is called:
questions.explain: Reaction formation is when an anxiety-laden impulse, thought, or feeling is replaced in consciousness by its opposite.

questions.q: When the ego fails to acknowledge the reality of threatening information, this defense mechanism is called:
questions.explain: Denial occurs when the ego is incapable of dealing with threatening facts and therefore fails to acknowledge their reality.

questions.q: Freud's theories are criticized as 'reductionist' because they reduce human behaviour to:
options: A basic set of abstract concepts
questions.explain: Freud's theories are criticized as reductionist because they reduce complex human behaviour to abstract concepts — the id, ego, and superego.

questions.q: A criticism of Freud's theories is that they were based on:
options: A very small, rather unique sample of people
questions.explain: Freud's theories were based on a very small, unique sample of people, limiting the generalisability of his conclusions.

questions.q: Freud believed that all thoughts and actions are determined by
options: forces in the personality that are often unconscious.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Freud's psychic determinism held that behaviour is driven by often-unconscious forces within the personality (id, ego, superego conflicts).

questions.q: Alfred Adler emphasized that humans are motivated to strive for:
questions.explain: Adler emphasized interpersonal and social factors, proposing that humans are motivated to strive for superiority and actively take part in this striving.

questions.q: Freud stressed the role of __________ in shaping our personalities.
options: our history of rewards and punishments
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Freud placed central importance on the unconscious mind in shaping personality and behaviour.

questions.q: Which of these is one of behaviourism's basic assumptions?
options: Behaviour is determined by the environment
Behaviour requires study of the mind, not observable actions
Behaviour is determined by unconscious conflict
questions.explain: A basic assumption of behaviourism is that behaviour is determined by the environment, and only observable behaviour should be studied.

questions.q: Behaviourists argue that behaviour can be reduced to:
questions.explain: Behaviourists argue all behaviour can be reduced to simple stimulus-response associations.

questions.q: A previously neutral stimulus that becomes linked with the UCS through repeated pairing, and elicits a conditioned response, is called the:
questions.explain: The conditioned stimulus (CS) is a previously neutral stimulus that becomes linked with the UCS through repeated pairing.

questions.q: Classical conditioning contributed to which therapeutic technique?
questions.explain: Classical conditioning principles brought about therapies such as systematic desensitisation.

questions.q: Operant conditioning, sometimes called instrumental learning, was first studied by which American psychologist?
questions.explain: Operant conditioning (instrumental learning) was first studied by American psychologist Edward Thorndike.

questions.q: Bandura's concept of learning through watching and copying another's actions, without direct reinforcement, is termed:
questions.explain: Vicarious learning is part of Bandura's observational learning theory — learning through observation and imitation, including modeling.

questions.q: Strict behaviorists were criticized for overlooking the role that __________ plays in our lives.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Strict behaviourism was criticized for ignoring internal cognitive processes like thinking, focusing only on observable stimulus-response behaviour.

questions.q: The key idea in the behavioristic view is that
options: behavior can be understood in terms of the mental processing of information.
environment plays a very small role in controlling one's behavior.
behavior is the result of clashing forces with the personality.
behavior is shaped and controlled by one's environment.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Behaviourism's central idea is that behaviour is shaped and controlled by the environment (through conditioning), not innate/internal forces.

questions.q: The humanistic viewpoint emphasizes
options: the idea that "the environment is the key causal matrix."
determinism, the unconscious, and biological drives.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Humanism centers on free will, self-image, and the drive toward self-actualization.

questions.q: According to the humanistic approach's basic assumptions, human beings are described as being:
options: Intentional, seeking meaning, value, and creativity
questions.explain: The humanistic approach holds that human beings are intentional — they seek meaning, value, and creativity, and cannot be reduced to simple components.

questions.q: Maslow proposed a need to develop one's potential and be the best one can be, which he called
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Self-actualization is Maslow's term for the need to fulfil one's own unique potential, at the top of his hierarchy of needs.

questions.q: Failure to satisfy love and belonging needs, per Maslow, can lead to:
options: Feelings of loneliness and social anxiety
questions.explain: Failure to satisfy love and belonging needs can lead to feelings of loneliness and social anxiety.

questions.q: Self-actualization was proposed by...
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Abraham Maslow proposed self-actualization as the pinnacle of his hierarchy of needs — the drive to fulfil one's fullest potential.

questions.q: Like Carl Rogers, I believe people choose to live more creative and meaningful lives. My name is
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Maslow, alongside Rogers, is a founding figure of humanistic psychology, which emphasizes free will and creative, meaningful living.

questions.q: Congruence/genuineness, one of Rogers' core therapeutic conditions, refers to:
options: The ability to be aware of inner experiences and let that be apparent in relationships
questions.explain: Congruence/genuineness is the basic ability to be aware of inner experiences and allow that inner experience to be apparent in relationships.

questions.q: According to Wilson et al. (1996), the humanistic approach is best described as:
options: A collection of diverse theories sharing optimism about human potential
questions.explain: Wilson et al. (1996) described the humanistic approach as not a comprehensive theory, but a collection of diverse theories with similar underlying principles, created by people optimistic about human potential.

questions.q: Cognitive theories are based mainly on which research setting?
questions.explain: Cognitive theories are based mainly on laboratory experiments, which is also part of the critique — that these are artificial environments.

questions.q: A key criticism of the cognitive approach is that it:
options: Cannot be tested using the scientific method
Focuses too heavily on innate drives
questions.explain: The cognitive approach is criticized for ignoring biology (e.g. hormones) and lacking the human element — ignoring social factors and emotion.

questions.q: A practitioner who is intensively trained in the theories of Freud and treats patients by talking to them is probably a
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. A psychoanalyst is specifically trained in Freudian theory and technique, treating patients through psychoanalytic talk therapy.

questions.q: Which part of the brain controls reflexes?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Simple reflexes are mediated by reflex arcs at the level of the spinal cord, allowing rapid responses without needing to involve the brain.

questions.q: Which part of the peripheral nervous system controls voluntary muscle activities, such as lifting a hand?
questions.explain: The somatic nervous system (SNS) controls voluntary activities such as lifting a hand to turn a page.

questions.q: Which branch of the autonomic nervous system prepares the body for emergencies, speeding up heart rate and suspending digestion?
questions.explain: The sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for emergencies or strenuous activity — speeding the heart, constricting/relaxing arteries, and suspending digestion.

questions.q: Which branch of the autonomic nervous system works to conserve energy and return the body to its normal resting state?
questions.explain: The parasympathetic nervous system conserves energy, reduces heart rate and blood pressure, and helps the body recover after strenuous activity.

questions.q: According to the all-or-none principle, when a neuron fires:
options: It fires at partial strength depending on stimulus size
It only fires once per minute
It fires at full strength every time
questions.explain: The all-or-none principle states that when a neuron fires, it does so at full strength; if not stimulated past threshold, it does not fire at all.

questions.q: Which part of a neuron receives impulses from other neurons and sends them to the cell body?
questions.explain: Dendrites are short, thin fibers that receive impulses from other neurons and send them toward the cell body.

questions.q: The white fatty substance that protects and insulates the axon, speeding transmission of impulses, is the:
questions.explain: The myelin sheath is a white fatty substance that insulates the axon and speeds transmission; its destruction (as in multiple sclerosis) causes erratic, uncoordinated behaviour.

questions.q: The gap between the axon terminals of one neuron and the dendrites of another neuron is called the:
questions.explain: The synapse is the gap between neurons across which neurotransmitters are released to transmit impulses.

questions.q: A child is frightened by a loud noise while playing with a cat. If the child learns to fear the cat, it can be said that the cat was
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. The cat, originally neutral, became associated with the loud noise (US) and came to elicit fear on its own — making it the CS.

questions.q: An undersupply of norepinephrine and serotonin may result in:
questions.explain: An undersupply of norepinephrine and serotonin may result in depression.

questions.q: A drug that blocks or inhibits a neurotransmitter's effect is called a(n):
questions.explain: An antagonist decreases or blocks the effect of a neurotransmitter; an agonist excites or increases its effect.

questions.q: Neurons that relay messages from the sense organs to the brain are called:
questions.explain: Afferent (sensory) neurons carry messages from sensory organs inward to the brain and spinal cord for processing.

questions.q: Which part of the hindbrain controls breathing, heart rate, and various reflexes?
questions.explain: The medulla, part of the hindbrain, controls breathing, heart rate, and a variety of reflexes.

questions.q: The brain structure that acts as a relay station, integrating almost all sensory input (except smell) on its way to the cortex, is the:
questions.explain: The thalamus integrates sensory input and acts as a relay station for information traveling to and from the cortex — all senses except smell pass through it.

questions.q: Which limbic system structure is important in the formation of memories?
questions.explain: The hippocampus is important in the formation of memories.

questions.q: The __________ is the part of the brain associated with fear and aggression.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. The amygdala, part of the limbic system, is centrally involved in processing fear and aggressive emotional responses.

questions.q: Which of these is most commonly associated with vision?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. The occipital lobe, at the back of the brain, is the primary visual processing centre.

questions.q: The lobe concerned with organization, planning, and creative thinking is the:
questions.explain: The frontal lobe is concerned with organization, planning, and creative thinking.

questions.q: Because of the discomfort and embarrassment associated with his childhood bedwetting, Andrew becomes nervous whenever he has the urge to urinate. If genital arousal subsequently makes Andrew unusually anxious, this would best illustrate:
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. The learned anxiety response spread from the original trigger (urge to urinate) to a similar physical sensation (genital arousal) — stimulus generalization.

questions.q: Which brain imaging technique is used to see which brain areas are activated while a person performs tasks?
questions.explain: Positron emission tomography (PET) shows which brain areas are activated during specific tasks, unlike CAT/MRI which mainly show structure.

questions.q: Which of the following is controlled by the thyroid gland?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. The thyroid gland produces thyroxine, which regulates the body's metabolic rate.

questions.q: Which gland is described as the 'master gland' because its secretions influence the release of hormones by other endocrine glands?
questions.explain: The pituitary gland is the master gland — it releases hormones influencing growth and triggers hormone release from other endocrine glands.

questions.q: The key difference between a hormone and a neurotransmitter is that a hormone is:
options: Released into the blood and diffuses throughout the body
questions.explain: A hormone is released into the blood and diffuses throughout the body, while a neurotransmitter is released right beside the cell it excites or inhibits.

questions.q: Twin studies help researchers determine the influence of genes on behaviour because identical twins:
options: Share the same genes as well as environment when raised together
questions.explain: Identical twins raised together share both genes and general environment; if they are more alike on a trait than fraternal twins, genetics likely plays a role in that trait.

questions.q: __________ focus their work on the attempt to explain all behavior in terms of internal physical mechanisms.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Biopsychologists attempt to explain behaviour through internal physical/biological mechanisms such as brain activity and neurochemistry.

questions.q: The parietal lobe is primarily concerned with:
options: Information from the senses from all over the body
questions.explain: The parietal lobe is concerned with information from the senses from all over the body.

questions.q: Research using brain lesions in animals found that removing certain brain parts made animals:
questions.explain: After removing part of the brain in experiments, animals that were fearful, aggressive, and vicious became less fearful and less violent, implying that brain area controlled aggression.

questions.q: A drug that excites or increases the effect of a neurotransmitter is called a(n):
questions.explain: An agonist excites or increases the effect of a neurotransmitter, while an antagonist decreases or blocks it.

questions.q: Transmission between neurons occurs whenever cells are stimulated:
options: Only in the presence of glucose
Past a minimum point, causing the cell to emit a signal
At any level, regardless of intensity
questions.explain: Transmission between neurons occurs whenever the cells are stimulated past a minimum point and emit a signal.

questions.q: Which hindbrain structure functions as a bridge between the spinal cord and the brain, and is involved in producing sleep-related chemicals?
questions.explain: The pons functions as a bridge between the spinal cord and brain, and is also involved in producing chemicals the body needs for sleep.

questions.q: The Reticular Activating System (RAS) is involved in alerting the brain to incoming signals and in regulating the:
questions.explain: The RAS serves to alert the rest of the brain to incoming signals, and is involved in the sleep/wake cycle.

questions.q: The nervous system controls all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Digestion of proteins in the stomach directly
questions.explain: The nervous system controls emotions, movements, thinking, and behaviour — direct protein digestion is a function of the digestive system, though it can be influenced indirectly.

questions.q: An injury to the spinal cord, which is protected by the vertebrae, could result in:
options: Paralysis, by preventing message transmission between brain and muscles
questions.explain: Because the bony protection of the spinal cord is vital, an injury could prevent transmittal of messages between brain and muscles, potentially causing paralysis.

questions.q: Someone is injured in an accident and he becomes irresponsible and develops impulsive behaviour. Which part of the brain is responsible?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. The frontal lobe governs planning, impulse control, and personality regulation — damage here classically produces impulsivity and irresponsibility (as in the famous case of Phineas Gage).

questions.q: According to the lecture, thinking, feeling, or acting without a body would be like:
questions.explain: The lecture states that to think, feel, or act without a body would be like running without legs — psychological experience is always simultaneously biological.

questions.q: Axon terminals are positioned opposite which structure of the next neuron?
questions.explain: Small fibers called axon terminals branch out at the end of the axon and are positioned opposite the dendrite of the next neuron.

questions.q: Endorphin's main role in the nervous system is to:
options: Inhibit pain or influence perception of pain/pleasure
questions.explain: Endorphin inhibits pain or influences the perception of pain or pleasure.

questions.q: The cerebral hemispheres are connected by a band of fibers called the:
questions.explain: The cerebral hemisphere is connected by a band of fibers called the corpus callosum.

questions.q: The sympathetic nervous system helps produce a 'runner's high' by:
options: Constricting some arteries and relaxing others to direct blood to muscles
questions.explain: The sympathetic nervous system constricts some arteries and relaxes others so blood flows to muscles where needed, sometimes producing a runner's high during strenuous activity.

questions.q: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) is primarily used to study:
questions.explain: MRI is an imaging technique used to study brain structure and activity.

questions.q: All sensory information, with one exception, enters the thalamus. Which sense is the exception?
questions.explain: All sensory information except smell enters the thalamus, which acts as a relay station to and from the cortex.

questions.q: The medulla, pons, and midbrain together compose most of the:
questions.explain: The medulla, pons, and midbrain compose most of the brain stem.

questions.q: The adrenal glands secrete epinephrine and norepinephrine, which heighten emotions such as:
questions.explain: Epinephrine and norepinephrine (adrenaline and noradrenaline) cause heartbeat/breathing to increase and heighten emotions such as fear and anxiety.

questions.q: Biopsychologists
options: attempt to explain behavior in terms of biological or physical mechanisms.
limit the scope of their study to animals.
are concerned with self-actualization and free will.
stress the unconscious aspect of behavior.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Biopsychologists focus on explaining behaviour through biological or physical mechanisms, such as brain function and genetics.

questions.q: The Autonomic Nervous System (ANS) controls activities that are:
options: Limited to reflex actions in the spinal cord
questions.explain: The ANS controls involuntary activities that ordinarily occur automatically, such as heartbeat, blood pressure, and pupil size.

questions.q: Hormones affect the growth of bodily structures such as muscles and bones, meaning they affect:
questions.explain: Hormones affect the growth of bodily structures such as muscles and bones, so they affect what you can do physically.

questions.q: Norepinephrine is involved with memory and learning, and also controls:
questions.explain: Norepinephrine is involved with memory and learning, and controls alertness and arousal.

questions.q: Cortical steroids, secreted by the adrenal glands, help muscles develop and cause the liver to:
options: Release stored sugar when extra energy is needed for emergencies
questions.explain: Cortical steroids help muscles develop and cause the liver to release stored sugar when the body requires extra energy for emergencies.

questions.q: Which part of the neuron contains the nucleus and produces energy needed to fuel neuron activity?
questions.explain: The cell body contains the nucleus and produces the energy needed to fuel neuron activity.

questions.q: An undersupply of acetylcholine is specifically associated with paralysis and which disease?
questions.explain: An undersupply of acetylcholine is associated with paralysis and Alzheimer's disease.

questions.q: Brain mechanisms involved in hunger and thirst would most likely be studied by a
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Biopsychologists study the biological/physiological mechanisms (like brain structures) underlying behaviours such as hunger and thirst.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT typically a concern of biological psychologists?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Biological psychologists study physiological processes like sleep, thirst, and hunger. Free will is a philosophical concept, not a physiological process, and falls outside biological psychology's typical scope.

questions.q: Under the brain's influence, the pituitary gland triggers the sex glands to release sex hormones, which in turn influence:
questions.explain: Under the brain's influence, the pituitary triggers the sex glands to release hormones, which in turn influence the brain and behaviour.

questions.q: GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) functions primarily as:
questions.explain: GABA is a major inhibitory neurotransmitter.

questions.q: Which brain imaging technique is specifically used to pinpoint injuries and brain deterioration?
questions.explain: CAT (computerized axial tomography) is used to study the brain to pinpoint injuries and brain deterioration.

questions.q: Glutamate, a major excitatory neurotransmitter, is especially involved in:
questions.explain: Glutamate is a major excitatory neurotransmitter, involved in memory.

questions.q: An undersupply of GABA is specifically linked to:
questions.explain: An undersupply of GABA is linked to seizures, tremors, and insomnia.

questions.q: Varying levels of estrogen and progesterone can cause which condition, with symptoms like fatigue, irritability, and depression?
questions.explain: Varying levels of estrogen and progesterone can cause premenstrual syndrome (PMS), with symptoms including fatigue, irritability, and depression.

questions.q: Genes are described in the lecture as the:
options: Basic units of heredity, reproduced and passed from parent to child
Structures found only in the brain
questions.explain: Genes are the basic units of heredity — they are reproduced and passed along from parent to child.

questions.q: The temporal lobe is concerned with hearing, memory, emotion, and:
questions.explain: The temporal lobe is concerned with hearing, memory, emotion, and speaking.

questions.q: A punisher can be
options: the onset of an unpleasant event
any consequence that reduces the occurrence of a behavior
the removal of a positive state of affairs
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. A punisher is defined functionally — any consequence that decreases the future occurrence of the behaviour it follows.

questions.q: Which area of the hypothalamus, when stimulated, causes the feeling of hunger; and when damaged, causes a person to never feel hungry again?
questions.explain: The lateral hypothalamus (LH), when stimulated, causes hunger; when damaged, a person would never feel hungry again and would likely lose weight.

questions.q: Overt behavior is
options: only those things which a person can see with his/her senses.
only those things a person does which you can see.
only those things which can be recorded by a camera.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Overt behaviour specifically refers to actions that are directly observable by others, distinguishing it from private, internal (covert) behaviour.

questions.q: Which hormone, made by fat cells, decreases appetite and signals the brain that the body has enough energy stores?
questions.explain: Leptin, made by fat cells, decreases appetite and signals to the brain that the body has sufficient energy stores.

questions.q: Which hormone increases appetite and is released primarily by the stomach to signal hunger to the brain?
questions.explain: Ghrelin increases appetite, is released mainly in the stomach, and rises before meals to signal hunger, then falls for about three hours after eating.

questions.q: Doing an activity purely for the pleasure or value of the activity itself, rather than for external reward, describes:
questions.explain: Intrinsic motivation is doing something for its own sake — for the pleasure or value inherent in the activity — not for an external reward.

questions.q: According to the lecture, which of the following is NOT one of the four factors driving intrinsic motivation?
questions.explain: The four factors of intrinsic motivation are autonomy, mastery, relatedness, and purpose — compliance is not one of them.

questions.q: On the first day of class Professor Wallace tells her history students that pop quizzes will be given at unpredictable times throughout the semester. Clearly, studying for Professor Wallace's surprise quizzes will be reinforced on a __________ schedule.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Since the quizzes occur at unpredictable points in time (not tied to a number of responses), studying is reinforced on a variable interval schedule.

questions.q: Some modern psychodynamic theorists, or neo-Freudians, focused on
options: human experience, problems, potentials, and ideals.
social motives and relationships that influence our behavior.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Neo-Freudians (e.g. Adler, Horney) shifted focus toward social motives and relationships as key influences on personality and behaviour.

questions.q: A state of internal tension that motivates an organism to act in ways that reduce that tension is called a:
questions.explain: A drive is an internal state of tension that motivates action to reduce the tension, tied to the concept of homeostasis.

questions.q: Which theory of motivation is built on the concept of homeostasis — organisms acting to reduce internal tension and restore physiological equilibrium?
questions.explain: Drive theory is based on homeostasis: individuals experiencing a drive are motivated to pursue actions that reduce that drive and restore equilibrium.

questions.q: Eating dessert after a large meal, even when not hungry, is a behaviour that challenges which theory of motivation?
questions.explain: Drive theory struggles to explain eating in the absence of internal tension (hunger), since it assumes people always act to reduce internal tension.

questions.q: An external reward or goal — such as a promotion or an 'A' grade — that has the capacity to motivate behaviour is called a(n):
questions.explain: An incentive is an external reward or goal with the capacity to motivate (or discourage) behaviour.

questions.q: According to the lecture, incentive theories differ from drive theories in that incentive theories locate the source of motivation:
questions.explain: Incentive theories emphasize external stimuli pulling behaviour, so the source of motivation lies outside the organism — unlike drive theories, where it lies within.

questions.q: Which theory of motivation emphasizes the environment and operant conditioning (rewards/punishments shaping behaviour) as the key driver?
questions.explain: Behaviorist theory of motivation emphasizes extrinsic, environmental contributions, grounded in operant conditioning.

questions.q: Maslow's humanistic theory of motivation proposes that the ultimate human motivator is:
questions.explain: Maslow proposed self-actualization — fulfilling one's true potential — as the ultimate human motivator, at the top of the needs hierarchy.

questions.q: According to arousal theory, when arousal levels drop too low (boredom), a person will typically:
options: Seek out stimulation to elevate arousal
questions.explain: Arousal theory holds that when arousal drops below one's optimal level, the person seeks out stimulation (e.g. going out with friends) to raise it again.

questions.q: Height and weight are positively correlated such that
options: Usually the taller one is, the thinner one is
As height increases, typically weight increases
There's no relationship between height and weight
Usually the shorter one is, the heavier the weight
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. A positive correlation means both variables tend to move in the same direction — as height increases, weight also tends to increase.

questions.q: Evolutionary theory of motivation proposes that natural selection favours behaviours and motives that:
options: Are entirely learned from the environment
questions.explain: Evolutionary (instinctual) theory proposes that natural selection favours behaviours and motives that maximize reproductive success — these are believed to be instinctual, fixed action patterns.

questions.q: Evolutionary psychologists would study
options: developmentally how chimpanzees and humans are similar.
historical behavior of a single species.
the biological makeup of the human mind across cultures.
male and female trends in mating choices.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Evolutionary psychology examines how behaviours have developed over the evolutionary history of a species, shaped by natural selection.

questions.q: Motives are best described as the needs, wants, and interests that:
questions.explain: Motives are the needs, wants, and interests that propel organisms in certain directions — what drives our actions.

questions.q: The forces that lie beneath motivation can be biological, social, emotional, or:
questions.explain: The forces beneath motivation can be biological, social, emotional, or cognitive in nature.

questions.q: Satiety is best defined as:
options: The absence of hunger; the sensation of feeling full
The physiological need to eat food
questions.explain: Satiety is the absence of hunger — the sensation of feeling full, in contrast to hunger.

questions.q: Behavior is
options: only those things which can be recorded by a camera.
only those things which a person can see with his/her senses.
only those things a person does which you can see.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Behaviour broadly refers to anything an organism does, encompassing both overt (observable) and covert (internal) actions.

questions.q: The paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus is also involved in:
questions.explain: Research shows the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus is also involved in hunger regulation, alongside the LH and VMH.

questions.q: Glucose is described in the lecture as:
options: A simple sugar that is an important source of energy
questions.explain: Glucose is a simple sugar which is an important source of energy; much of the food we eat is converted to glucose.

questions.q: Activities that decrease blood sugar level tend to:
questions.explain: Activities that decrease blood sugar level can increase hunger, while those that increase blood sugar can make people feel full.

questions.q: Glucostats are described as:
options: A part of the digestive tract
Neurons sensitive to glucose in the surrounding fluid
questions.explain: Glucostats are neurons sensitive to glucose in the surrounding fluid, monitoring fluctuations in blood glucose level.

questions.q: After food is consumed, which nerve carries information about the stretching of the stomach wall, indicating fullness?
questions.explain: The vagus nerve carries information about the stretching of the stomach wall after eating, which indicates when the stomach is full.

questions.q: Many obese people don't respond to leptin's signals even though they:
options: Have higher levels of leptin in their blood
questions.explain: Many obese people don't respond to leptin's signals even though they have higher levels of leptin, a phenomenon known as leptin resistance.

questions.q: If you have a snake phobia because you once heard a loud noise while looking at a snake, for you a snake is a(n)
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. The snake, originally neutral, became paired with the loud noise (US) and now elicits fear on its own — making it a conditioned stimulus (CS).

questions.q: The APA professional code stresses
options: cooperation with authorities when a client is suspected of a crime.
deception as a technique to engage the psyche.
use of the scientific method in testing hypotheses.
high levels of competence, integrity, and responsibility.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. The American Psychological Association's ethics code emphasizes competence, integrity, and responsibility in professional practice.

questions.q: The lecture identifies intrinsic motivation as the only path to what kind of motivation?
questions.explain: According to the lecture, the only path to sustainable, long-term motivation is through intrinsic motivation.

questions.q: 'Mastery', one of the four intrinsic motivation factors, refers to people wanting to:
options: Get better at what they do
Have control over their life and activities
Be part of something greater than themselves
questions.explain: Mastery refers to people wanting to get better at what they do — one of the four factors driving intrinsic motivation.

questions.q: 'Relatedness', one of the four intrinsic motivation factors, refers to people wanting to:
questions.explain: Relatedness refers to people wanting to feel connected to other people.

questions.q: 'Purpose', one of the four intrinsic motivation factors, refers to people wanting to:
options: Get better at what they do
Be part of something greater than themselves
questions.explain: Purpose refers to people wanting to be part of something greater than themselves.

questions.q: A loud noise startles you and makes you jump. As it occurs several times, you jump less and less each time. This is an example of
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. A decreasing response to a repeated, harmless stimulus is habituation — a simple, non-associative form of learning.

questions.q: Biological motives include hunger, thirst, temperature, sleep, rest, and:
questions.explain: Biological motives include hunger, thirst, temperature, sleep, rest, and similar essential, survival-related bodily needs.

questions.q: Compared to biological needs, people can acquire social needs that are:
options: Identical across all individuals in strength
Unlimited in number, through learning and socializing
questions.explain: People have a limited number of biological needs but can acquire an unlimited number of social needs from learning and socializing.

questions.q: How many major theories of motivation are outlined in the lecture?
questions.explain: The lecture outlines six theories: drive theory, incentive theory, behaviorist theory, humanistic theory, arousal theory, and evolutionary theory.

questions.q: States of tension described in drive theory are said to be unpleasant and:
questions.explain: States of tension (drives) are unpleasant and disrupt the preferred equilibrium (homeostasis).

questions.q: According to the lecture's example, eating dessert after already being full demonstrates that motivation may exist:
options: Only in the absence of incentives
questions.explain: Motivation may exist without drive arousal — eating dessert after already being full is not driven by hunger tension.

questions.q: Incentives can be used to get people to engage in certain behaviours, as well as to get people to:
questions.explain: Incentives can be used both to encourage certain behaviours and to get people to stop performing certain actions.

questions.q: Using poker chips to reinforce mental patients for healthy behavior would be an example of using
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Poker chips exchangeable for privileges are a classic example of a token economy.

questions.q: Which of the following is the best example of covert behavior?
options: blinking in response to a light
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Covert behaviour is internal and not directly observable by others — remembering something is a private, internal mental event.

questions.q: Incentive theories emphasize environmental factors and downplay:
options: The biological basis for human motivation
questions.explain: Incentive theories emphasize environmental factors and downplay the biological basis for human motivation.

questions.q: One of the foundations of behaviourist theory of motivation is the idea of operant conditioning, where:
options: Arousal must be kept at zero
Rewards and punishments shape future behaviour
questions.explain: One foundation of behaviourist theory of motivation is operant conditioning, where rewards and punishments shape future behaviour.

questions.q: In Maslow's hierarchy applied to motivation, the level below a need must generally be satisfied before:
options: A person experiences any deficiency needs
Any growth needs can ever be considered
A person can move upwards to the next level
questions.explain: In Maslow's hierarchy, the level below must be satisfied before a person can move upwards to the next level.

questions.q: Which of the following might serve as a secondary reinforcer?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Grades are a learned (secondary) reinforcer, acquiring their reinforcing value through association — unlike food or sex, which are primary/innate reinforcers.

questions.q: Arousal theory shares commonalities with drive-reduction theory but differs by suggesting we are motivated to:
options: Maintain an ideal level of arousal, not just reduce tension
questions.explain: Unlike drive-reduction theory's focus on reducing tension, arousal theory suggests we are motivated to maintain an ideal level of arousal.

questions.q: To shape the behavior of their students, teachers employ
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Teachers commonly use secondary reinforcers (praise, grades, stickers) to shape student behaviour.

questions.q: Evolutionary theory of motivation is also known as:
questions.explain: Because evolutionary theory proposes true instincts as stereotypical fixed action patterns, it is also known as instinctual theory.

questions.q: Which of the following behaviours is listed as an example under evolutionary theory of motivation?
options: Aggression, dominance, attraction, affiliation, achievement, and curiosity
questions.explain: Evolutionary theory includes behaviours such as aggression, dominance, attraction, affiliation, achievement, and curiosity as instinctual.

questions.q: According to evolutionary theory, dominant males may 'poach' females from subordinate males and intimidate rivals, illustrating competition for:
options: Social status with no reproductive link
questions.explain: Dominant males poaching females and intimidating rivals illustrates competition for sexual (reproductive) success, as described in evolutionary theory.

questions.q: In the business world application, tying compensation incentives directly to performance objectives is an example of applying which theory?
questions.explain: Using commission pay to tie compensation directly to performance objectives is an application of incentive theory in the business world.

questions.q: The first grade teacher gives students stickers when they perform well. If they earn five stickers in one day they are exempt from homework. The stickers in this example could also be called
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Stickers exchangeable for a reward (homework exemption) function as tokens — a form of secondary/generalized reinforcer.

questions.q: In __________ reinforcement, the reinforcer follows every correct response.
questions.explain: Continuous reinforcement means every correct response is reinforced, unlike partial/intermittent schedules where only some responses are reinforced.

questions.q: In Pavlov's experiments with dogs, salivation was the
questions.explain: Salivation to food is an innate, reflexive reaction — an unconditioned response. (It only becomes a conditioned response once elicited by the bell alone.)

questions.q: The presentation of an aversive stimulus or the removal of a positive stimulus are both examples of
questions.explain: Presenting something aversive is positive punishment; removing something pleasant is negative punishment — both decrease behaviour, so both are forms of punishment.

questions.q: In classical conditioning, learning is evident when a
options: subject repeats an action he or she has observed in another and is praised for it
stimulus automatically produces a response without a prior history of experience
spontaneously emitted response increases in frequency as a result of its consequences
stimulus which did not initially produce a response now elicits that response
questions.explain: Classical conditioning is demonstrated when a previously neutral stimulus comes to elicit a response it did not originally produce.

questions.q: In Thorndike's law of effect, events critical for conditioning
options: are unrelated to the response except during extinction
questions.explain: The law of effect concerns consequences (reward/punishment) that follow a response, strengthening or weakening it — these occur after the response.

questions.q: If you have a snake phobia because you once heard a loud noise while looking at a snake, for you a snake is a(n)
questions.explain: The snake, originally neutral, became paired with the loud noise (US) and now elicits fear on its own — making it a conditioned stimulus (CS).

questions.q: A series of responses that gradually approach a desired pattern of behavior are called
questions.explain: Successive approximations are the small steps gradually shaped toward a final target behaviour, the basis of the shaping procedure.

questions.q: If the conditioned stimulus is presented many times without reinforcement, we can expect
options: the strength of the UR to increase
questions.explain: Repeated presentation of the CS without pairing it with the US weakens and eventually eliminates the conditioned response — extinction.

questions.q: A child has learned to avoid a furry, black cat. However, she still plays with her grandmother's short-haired tabby. Her response demonstrates
questions.explain: Responding differently to similar but distinguishable stimuli (avoiding one cat but not another) is stimulus discrimination.

questions.q: Punishment is most effective in suppressing behavior when it is
questions.explain: Punishment works best when delivered right after the behaviour, applied every time, and strong enough to be aversive.

questions.q: The greatest degree of resistance to extinction is typically caused by a __________ schedule of reinforcement.
questions.explain: Variable ratio schedules (reward after an unpredictable number of responses, as in gambling) produce the greatest resistance to extinction of all schedules — this is the classic textbook answer, and matches Q26's point that gambling addiction stems from partial/variable-ratio reinforcement.

questions.q: In Pavlov's experiments with dogs, the conditioned stimulus was the
questions.explain: The bell, originally neutral, became the conditioned stimulus once it was paired repeatedly with food.

questions.q: Ivan Pavlov has been credited with the initial discovery of
questions.explain: Pavlov's work on salivary conditioning in dogs is the foundation of classical conditioning.

questions.q: In Pavlov's experiments with dogs, the bell (prior to conditioning) was the
questions.explain: Before conditioning began, the bell produced no relevant response — making it a neutral stimulus.

questions.q: Reinforcement in operant conditioning is most effective when it is
questions.explain: Operant reinforcement works best when delivered contingent on (dependent on) the specific response occurring.

questions.q: After pairing the CS and US in a series of conditioning trials, the organism learns to respond to the CS alone. This response is then called
questions.explain: The learned response to the CS alone, after conditioning, is the conditioned response (CR).

questions.q: Jimmy helps his father put away the dishes after dinner. Jimmy's father wants to increase the probability of this behavior and will be most successful by praising Jimmy
options: after all the dishes are put away
the next time they are putting away dishes
questions.explain: Reinforcement is most effective when delivered immediately after the target behaviour — right after the dishes are put away.

questions.q: After a response has been extinguished, it will often reappear after a short time has passed. This is called
questions.explain: Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of an extinguished response after a rest period, without any further conditioning trials.

questions.q: The first grade teacher gives students stickers when they perform well. If they earn five stickers in one day they are exempt from homework. The stickers in this example could also be called
questions.explain: Stickers exchangeable for a reward (homework exemption) function as tokens — a form of secondary/generalized reinforcer.

questions.q: A student does a good job on math problems for homework, and the teacher awards a sticker. This demonstrates the use of
questions.explain: Awarding a sticker for good performance, which increases the likelihood of the behaviour recurring, is reinforcement.

questions.q: In Pavlov's experiments with dogs, the bell (during and after conditioning) was the
questions.explain: Once conditioning occurred, the bell reliably elicited salivation on its own, making it the conditioned stimulus.

questions.q: One difference between classical and operant conditioning is that
options: classical conditioning involves learning in which antecedent events are associated with one another
operant conditioning involves learning in which antecedent events are associated with one another
operant conditioning occurs when a response is not affected by consequences
animals learn only by operant conditioning
questions.explain: Classical conditioning links two antecedent stimuli (CS and US) together; operant conditioning links a response to its consequence.

questions.q: In classical conditioning, events critical to the learning occur __________ the response.
questions.explain: In classical conditioning, the critical pairing (CS with US) occurs before the response is elicited.

questions.q: A punisher can be
options: any consequence that reduces the occurrence of a behavior
the removal of a positive state of affairs
the onset of an unpleasant event
questions.explain: A punisher is defined functionally — any consequence that decreases the future occurrence of the behaviour it follows.

questions.q: In a study of punishment, shock is administered to a hamster through a wire grid on the bottom of the cage. To the researcher's surprise, the hamster learns to roll on its back when shocked so that its fur insulates it from the shock. The hamster's response demonstrates
questions.explain: Rolling over removes/reduces the aversive shock sensation, so the behaviour is strengthened through negative reinforcement (escape learning).

questions.q: Becoming addicted to gambling is related to the effects of
questions.explain: Gambling pays out on an unpredictable (variable ratio) partial reinforcement schedule, which is highly resistant to extinction — driving persistent, addictive behaviour.

questions.q: The technique of using desensitization involves
options: flooding the person with images of the feared stimulus
systematically increasing the stimulus intensity up to the breaking point
gradually exposing the person to the feared stimulus
gradually exposing the person to the feared stimulus only when they are fully relaxed
questions.explain: Systematic desensitisation pairs gradual exposure to a feared stimulus with a relaxed state, so relaxation counter-conditions the fear response.

questions.q: A dog that gets rewarded for the first bark it makes in each ten minute period is being reinforced on a __________ schedule of reinforcement.
questions.explain: Reward is available for the first correct response after a fixed period of time (10 minutes) — a fixed interval schedule.

questions.q: In Pavlov's experiments with dogs, food was the
questions.explain: Food naturally and automatically triggers salivation without any learning, making it the unconditioned stimulus.

questions.q: To strengthen the connection between the CS and the CR, the CS must
questions.explain: For conditioning to occur effectively, the CS must come before the US, signalling its arrival.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about punishment is FALSE?
options: Punishment may permanently suppress a response
questions.explain: Punishment only suppresses an existing unwanted response — it does not teach the individual a new, desired behaviour to replace it. That's a key limitation of punishment.

questions.q: Operant conditioning was studied by
questions.explain: B. F. Skinner is most closely associated with the systematic study of operant conditioning (building on Thorndike's earlier law of effect).

questions.q: Using poker chips to reinforce mental patients for healthy behavior would be an example of using
questions.explain: Poker chips exchangeable for privileges are a classic example of a token economy.

questions.q: Advertisers often try to use higher order conditioning by
options: reducing fear or anxiety as they repeatedly show the same commercial
associating the unconditioned stimulus with a cognitive response
pairing images that evoke good feelings with pictures of their products
sounding loud tones at key points in the advertisement
questions.explain: Higher-order conditioning pairs an already-established CS (an image evoking good feelings) with a new stimulus (the product) to transfer that positive response.

questions.q: A neutral stimulus is one that
options: leads to an increase of the UR
leads to a decrease of the UR
depends on the size of the UR
questions.explain: Before conditioning, a neutral stimulus produces no relevant response at all — it does not evoke the unconditioned response.

questions.q: Which of the following might serve as a secondary reinforcer?
questions.explain: Grades are a learned (secondary) reinforcer, acquiring their reinforcing value through association — unlike food or sex, which are primary/innate reinforcers.

questions.q: For conditioning to occur, the proper order of events is
questions.explain: The CS is presented, then the US follows, which produces the (unconditioned) response — CS then US then UR, before the CR eventually emerges.

questions.q: A team coach who benches a player for poor performance is using
questions.explain: Removing a privilege (playing time) to decrease the poor-performance behaviour is negative punishment.

questions.q: In operant conditioning, what is the relationship between events critical to learning and the response to be learned?
options: They are unrelated to the response
They occur simultaneously with the response
questions.explain: In operant conditioning, the consequence (reinforcement/punishment) that drives learning occurs after the response.

questions.q: The unconditioned stimulus, by definition, leads to a(n)
questions.explain: By definition, the unconditioned stimulus naturally and automatically elicits the unconditioned response, without any learning required.

questions.q: In a classic experiment, "Little Albert," a very young boy, was conditioned to be afraid of a rat. He also became fearful of white furry rabbits and bearded men. This is an example of
questions.explain: The fear response spread to similar stimuli (furry, white objects) — a textbook case of stimulus generalization.

questions.q: When a stimulus acquires the power to elicit a response as a result of being paired with a stimulus that already produces the response
