questions.explain: This describes the basic definition of classical conditioning — pairing a neutral stimulus with one that already elicits a response.

questions.q: Which of the following describes the state of affairs after conditioning?
questions.explain: After conditioning is complete, the CS alone now elicits the (conditioned) response — CS-CR.

questions.q: The most basic form of learning that is not heavily dependent on higher order intellectual processes is known as
questions.explain: Conditioning (classical and operant) is considered a basic associative form of learning, not requiring complex reasoning.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes punishment?
questions.explain: Punishment, in its most basic (positive punishment) form, is the addition of an aversive event following a behaviour to decrease it.

questions.q: Negative reinforcement __________ responding; punishment __________ responding.
questions.explain: Negative reinforcement strengthens/increases a behaviour (by removing something aversive); punishment weakens/decreases a behaviour.

questions.q: Two schedules of reinforcement that produce the highest rates of response are
questions.explain: Ratio schedules (based on number of responses, not time) generally produce the highest rates of responding — both fixed ratio and variable ratio.

questions.q: __________ occurs when making a response removes an unpleasant event.
questions.explain: Negative reinforcement is when a response removes or avoids an unpleasant stimulus, increasing the likelihood of that response.

questions.q: To shape the behavior of their students, teachers employ
questions.explain: Teachers commonly use secondary reinforcers (praise, grades, stickers) to shape student behaviour.

questions.q: If you give a child her favorite licorice candy for doing well in school and she continues to do well in school, the licorice candy is
options: neither a reinforcer nor a reward
a reward, but not a reinforcer
a reinforcer, but not a reward
questions.explain: Since the candy is pleasant (a reward) and it actually increased the behaviour (functioning as a reinforcer), it qualifies as both.

questions.q: Increased feedback…………….
options: has no effect on learning and performance
almost always improves learning and performance
is not as effective as computer-assisted learning
questions.explain: More frequent, informative feedback almost always improves learning and performance by helping learners correct errors.

questions.q: A child is conditioned to fear a furry, black cat. Soon she becomes fearful of any black, furry object. Her new response demonstrates
questions.explain: The fear spreading to similar (black, furry) stimuli is a clear example of stimulus generalization.

questions.q: The schedule of reinforcement in which a set number of responses must be made for each reward is called
questions.explain: A fixed ratio schedule requires a set, unchanging number of responses before each reward is given.

questions.q: The fact that responses become more resistant to extinction, after partial reinforcement, is called
questions.explain: This well-known phenomenon — partially reinforced behaviours are harder to extinguish than continuously reinforced ones — is called the partial reinforcement effect.

questions.q: If you slow down every time you see a police car, your slowing down is probably due to
questions.explain: Slowing down helps you avoid (escape) the possibility of a ticket — an aversive consequence — making this negative reinforcement.

questions.q: Your niece has a temper tantrum in the store when she is shopping. If you buy her a toy you are
questions.explain: Rewarding the tantrum with a toy reinforces that behaviour, making future tantrums more likely.

questions.q: Negative reinforcement and punishment
options: are not very effective in changing behavior
are different terms for the same procedure
have the same effect on behavior
questions.explain: Negative reinforcement increases behaviour; punishment decreases behaviour — they have opposite effects, despite both involving aversive stimuli.

questions.q: A puppy has begun to cry and bark in order to be let into the house. To extinguish this response, you would
options: swat the puppy with a newspaper whenever it cried
let the puppy in when it cries, then swat it with a newspaper
let the puppy in the house
ignore the crying, letting the puppy in when quiet
questions.explain: Extinction requires withholding the reinforcer (letting the puppy in) for the unwanted behaviour, and instead rewarding the desired behaviour (being quiet).

questions.q: Acquiring a fear of a light because you saw someone else getting shocked when the light came on is an example of
questions.explain: Learning an emotional response by observing what happens to someone else, rather than experiencing it directly, is vicarious conditioning.

questions.q: Secondary reinforcers are
options: much more effective than primary reinforcers
questions.explain: Unlike primary reinforcers (innately rewarding, like food), secondary reinforcers (like money or grades) acquire their value through learning/association.

questions.q: Which form of learning would most likely be studied in a Skinner box?
questions.explain: The Skinner box was designed specifically to study operant conditioning — how consequences shape voluntary behaviour.

questions.q: A child is frightened by a loud noise while playing with a cat. If the child learns to fear the cat, it can be said that the cat was
questions.explain: The cat, originally neutral, became associated with the loud noise (US) and came to elicit fear on its own — making it the CS.

questions.q: A child bitten by a white dog is not afraid of black dogs. This is an example of
questions.explain: Responding with fear to one specific stimulus (white dogs) but not a similar one (black dogs) is stimulus discrimination.

questions.q: Presenting the conditioned stimulus without the unconditioned stimulus will result in
questions.explain: Repeatedly presenting the CS alone, without the US, weakens the association and leads to extinction of the conditioned response.

questions.q: A corporate pay policy comparable to a fixed ratio schedule of reinforcement is
options: salary adjustments based on the quality of work performed
paying employees at the end of each day
payment of employees on a piece-work basis
questions.explain: Piece-work pay (a fixed amount per unit produced) mirrors a fixed ratio schedule — reward tied to a set number of responses.

questions.q: By a continuous reinforcement schedule, we mean that
options: responding without pausing is the requirement for reinforcement
reinforcements occur continuously regardless of the subject's behavior
reinforcement continues even when errors are made
questions.explain: Continuous reinforcement means every single correct response receives reinforcement, with no responses left unreinforced.

questions.q: When you are first learning golf, you may hit one or two great shots in an entire round. You are being reinforced on what kind of partial reinforcement schedule?
questions.explain: Good shots occur unpredictably relative to the number of swings taken — an unpredictable number of responses per reward is a variable ratio schedule.

questions.q: To teach a child to eat spaghetti, you would reinforce initial responses, such as holding the fork, and then increasingly closer approximations to the final response, a procedure known as
questions.explain: Reinforcing successive approximations toward a final target behaviour is the definition of shaping.

questions.q: A rat learns to push a button in order to turn on a tone previously associated with food. The button pushing has been rewarded by a(n) __________ reinforcer.
questions.explain: The tone itself isn't inherently rewarding — it only became reinforcing through its association with food, making it a secondary (conditioned) reinforcer.

questions.q: Your handsome successful boyfriend winks at you each time before he tells you "I love you." Your expectation when he winks is a(an)
questions.explain: The learned feeling/expectation triggered by the wink (a previously neutral cue, now paired with an emotional statement) is a conditioned response.

questions.q: The process through which a response is taught by rewarding successive approximations to the final desired response is
questions.explain: This is the definition of shaping — building a complex behaviour step by step through reinforcement of closer and closer approximations.

questions.q: A child who occasionally gets rewarded with candy after asking her grandmother for a "treat" is being rewarded on a __________ schedule.
questions.explain: Unpredictable rewards for an unpredictable number of requests describe a variable ratio schedule.

questions.q: Teaching your cat to turn on the living room lights would best be accomplished by
questions.explain: A complex, unnatural behaviour like this would need to be built gradually through shaping — reinforcing successive approximations.

questions.q: In operant conditioning, the reinforcer occurs __________ the response, and in classical conditioning, it occurs __________.
questions.explain: In operant conditioning the reinforcer follows the response; in classical conditioning, the critical pairing (CS-US) occurs before the response is elicited.

questions.q: Two principles of conditioning that have aided our learning and improved our adaptability as a species are
options: lower order and higher order conditioning
questions.explain: Generalization lets us respond appropriately to similar new situations, while discrimination lets us respond differently to distinct ones — together, these adaptively shape behaviour.

questions.q: Learning is best defined as
options: a relatively permanent change in behavior due to past experience
any change in behavior caused by punishment
a permanent change in behavior due to physical development
questions.explain: The standard definition of learning excludes temporary changes (fatigue) and changes from maturation — it must be a relatively permanent change due to experience.

questions.q: Responses that are reinforced and tend to be repeated illustrate
questions.explain: The strengthening of a response because of its reinforcing consequences is the core principle of operant conditioning.

questions.q: To be effective, punishment should be
options: explained in detail to the child
questions.explain: Punishment is most effective when paired with reinforcement of an alternative, desired behaviour — teaching what TO do, not just what not to do.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the unusual events that occurred in Pavlov's laboratory leading him to the discovery of classical conditioning?
options: Dogs sometimes salivated before meat powder was placed in their mouths
Dogs salivated if and only if they were given a reward
Salivation existed in dogs as an unlearned reflex
Dogs salivated after meat powder was placed in their mouths
questions.explain: Pavlov's discovery began when he noticed dogs salivating in anticipation, before the food itself was presented — this anomaly led him to investigate conditioning.

questions.q: After weeks of successful extinction trials, your pet dachshund suddenly resumes burying bones in the front yard. Your pet therapist advises you that the dog's behavior is an example of
questions.explain: The reappearance of a previously extinguished behaviour after some time has passed is spontaneous recovery.

questions.q: Operant conditioning is to Skinner as classical conditioning is to
questions.explain: Just as Skinner is associated with operant conditioning, Pavlov is the founding figure of classical conditioning.

questions.q: Classical conditioning is most often used to condition
questions.explain: Classical conditioning works on involuntary, reflexive responses (like salivation or fear reactions), not voluntary/operant behaviours.

questions.q: Jason experiences nicotine withdrawal symptoms (e.g., a slight headache) after he has not smoked a cigarette for 20 minutes. When he smokes another cigarette, this symptom disappears, but then reoccurs 20 minutes later when he must smoke still another cigarette to make his headache go away again. Which of the following operant conditioning terms best explains why Jason continues to smoke, even though he knows nonsmokers live an average of 10 years longer than smokers?
questions.explain: Smoking removes the aversive withdrawal headache, so the behaviour (smoking) is strengthened by escaping an unpleasant state — negative reinforcement.

questions.q: A second grade student loses 1 minute of recess every time she breaks a classroom rule. Eventually, the student stops breaking the classroom rules. This is an example of
questions.explain: Losing recess time removes a pleasant privilege following the unwanted behaviour, decreasing it — negative punishment.

questions.q: You are potty training Ama, your 3 year old sister. She lets you know every time she needs to use the bathroom, however she is having accidents instead of actually using the toilet. Her pediatrician suggests that you should have her clean underwear every time she has an accident. You start enforcing this rule, and she has fewer accidents. This is an example of…
questions.explain: Adding an unpleasant task (cleaning her own underwear) after the unwanted behaviour, which decreases it, is positive punishment.

questions.q: You are absent from school for an afternoon. When you return, you read the report left by your substitute. Her report states that half of your class behaved wonderfully and completed their entire assignment. The other half of the class misbehaved and did not finish their assignment. For the students who behaved, you give them free time on the computer. For the students who misbehaved, you give them an extra, more difficult assignment to accomplish. In this situation you provided…
questions.explain: Free computer time adds something pleasant (positive reinforcement) for good behaviour; the extra, harder assignment adds something aversive (positive punishment) for misbehaviour.

questions.q: When a previously reinforced behavior is no longer reinforced and its rate of occurrence decreases, what behavioral principle is being used?
questions.explain: Withholding reinforcement for a previously reinforced behaviour, causing it to fade, is the definition of extinction.

questions.q: The Law of Effect is associated with what behavioral principle?
questions.explain: Thorndike's law of effect states that responses followed by satisfying consequences are strengthened — the basic principle behind (positive) reinforcement.

questions.q: Three of the following are examples of positive reinforcement. Which one is (are) NOT? (Alice is praised but vows never to act smart again; Bart keeps a new javelin technique because it goes farther; Cordell becomes the class clown after his jokes get laughs; Donna starts getting frequent 'stomach aches' after discovering it gets her out of PE early)
questions.explain: Since the praise led Alice to vow to NEVER repeat the smart behaviour, her target behaviour actually decreased — meaning the praise did not function as positive reinforcement for her, unlike the other three cases where the target behaviour increased.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example(s) of "negative reinforcement"? (Eric is seen as cool for swearing; Ophelia finishes her paper early so it stops hanging over her head; Timothy is scolded for hiding a magazine; Myra gets attention for wearing tight outfits)
questions.explain: Finishing the paper early removes the unpleasant feeling of an unfinished task hanging over her — escaping an aversive state is negative reinforcement. The other cases involve adding a pleasant consequence (positive reinforcement) or an aversive one (punishment).

questions.q: Sally has trouble sitting still in class. Mr. Amoah begins praising Sally whenever she sits quietly, and her behaviour improves. He eventually stops reinforcing her since she's behaving as well as her classmates, but by January her restless behaviour has returned. From an operant conditioning perspective, what should Mr. Amoah have done differently?
options: He should have punished her for getting out of her seat and other 'restless' behaviours.
He should have continued to reinforce her for sitting quietly on an intermittent basis.
He should have used a reinforcer other than praise.
He should have taught Sally to discriminate between situations where sitting still was and wasn't appropriate.
questions.explain: Behaviour maintained through reinforcement tends to fade once reinforcement stops abruptly. Shifting to intermittent (partial) reinforcement, rather than cutting it off entirely, maintains the behaviour long-term with much greater resistance to extinction.

questions.q: A supervisor comes into the workplace to check on her employees every hour and a half. An observer notices that the workers increase their work behavior about 10 minutes before the supervisor arrives and then decrease their work behavior after she leaves. On what type of reinforcement schedule are the workers?
questions.explain: Checks occur at a predictable, fixed time interval (every 1.5 hours); the classic 'scallop' pattern — a burst of activity right before the check and a drop right after — is the signature of a fixed interval schedule.

questions.q: Kobina's mother has been nagging him for weeks to clean the garage. When he does so, his mother's nagging ceases. Kobina's mother's nagging was a
questions.explain: The nagging was an aversive stimulus whose removal (once Kobina cleaned the garage) reinforced the cleaning behaviour — making the nagging itself a negative reinforcer.

questions.q: Taking an aspirin every day to reduce one's chances of a heart attack is an example of a behaviour controlled by
questions.explain: Taking the aspirin avoids or reduces the likelihood of a future aversive event (a heart attack), which is negative reinforcement.

questions.q: Response-stimulus associations are to __________ as stimulus-stimulus associations are to __________.
questions.explain: Operant conditioning links a response to its consequence (response-stimulus); classical conditioning links two stimuli together (stimulus-stimulus).

questions.q: Last year, Dr. Agyapong cleaned Akua's skin with rubbing alcohol prior to administering each of a series of painful rabies vaccination shots. Which of the following processes accounts for the fact that Akua currently becomes fearful every time she smells rubbing alcohol?
questions.explain: The smell of rubbing alcohol, originally neutral, became associated with the painful shots and now elicits fear on its own — classical conditioning.

questions.q: Because of the discomfort and embarrassment associated with his childhood bedwetting, Andrew becomes nervous whenever he has the urge to urinate. If genital arousal subsequently makes Andrew unusually anxious, this would best illustrate:
questions.explain: The learned anxiety response spread from the original trigger (urge to urinate) to a similar physical sensation (genital arousal) — stimulus generalization.

questions.q: Because Andrew was spanked on several occasions for biting electric cords, he no longer does so. Andrew's behavior change best illustrates the value of:
questions.explain: An aversive consequence (spanking) following a behaviour, which decreases that behaviour, is operant conditioning (specifically, punishment).

questions.q: The study of respondent behavior is to __________ as the study of operant behavior is to __________.
questions.explain: Respondent (classical) conditioning is associated with Pavlov; operant conditioning is associated with Skinner.

questions.q: Because Carol would always pick up her newborn daughter when she began to cry, her daughter is now a real crybaby. In this case, picking up the infant served as a(n) __________ for crying.
questions.explain: Picking up the infant is a pleasant consequence added after crying that increased the crying behaviour — a positive reinforcer.

questions.q: Positive reinforcers __________ the rate of operant responding, and negative reinforcers __________ the rate of operant responding.
questions.explain: Both positive and negative reinforcers strengthen (increase) the behaviour they follow — that's what makes them both forms of reinforcement, as opposed to punishment.

questions.q: Julie drinks alcohol in the early evening because it relieves her anxiety. Her drinking is likely to continue because it is followed by a __________ reinforcer.
questions.explain: The drinking removes an unpleasant state (anxiety), so it is maintained through negative reinforcement.

questions.q: When the Boatengs eat dinner, the family dog begs for food. Sometimes, but not often, the children give in to the dog's begging and pass their pet a tasty morsel. You would be most justified in predicting that:
options: The dog is going to be quite persistent in its begging in the future.
As soon as the children stop reinforcing the dog's begging, it will stop begging.
The dog is eventually going to stop begging for food.
The dog will always beg for food even if the Boatengs never reinforce the begging.
questions.explain: Occasional, unpredictable rewards (partial/intermittent reinforcement) build behaviour that is highly persistent and resistant to extinction — the dog will keep begging persistently.

questions.q: Joe is a house painter who wants to be paid for each square foot of surface he completes rather than with an hourly wage. Joe prefers working on a ________ schedule of reinforcement.
questions.explain: Pay tied to a fixed, set amount of output (square footage completed) is a fixed ratio schedule.

questions.q: Paul and Michael sell magazine subscriptions by telephone. Paul is paid $1.00 for every 5 calls he makes, regardless of the number of sales, while Michael is paid $1 for every subscription he sells, regardless of the number of calls he makes. Paul's telephoning is reinforced on a __________ schedule, while Michael's is reinforced on a __________ schedule.
questions.explain: Paul is paid after a fixed number of calls (5) — fixed ratio. Michael is paid per sale, but the number of calls needed to make a sale varies unpredictably — variable ratio.

questions.q: Gamblers who insert coins in a slot machine are reinforced on a __________ schedule.
questions.explain: Slot machine payouts occur after an unpredictable number of plays — the classic variable ratio schedule.

questions.q: On the first day of class Professor Wallace tells her history students that pop quizzes will be given at unpredictable times throughout the semester. Clearly, studying for Professor Wallace's surprise quizzes will be reinforced on a __________ schedule.
questions.explain: Since the quizzes occur at unpredictable points in time (not tied to a number of responses), studying is reinforced on a variable interval schedule.

questions.q: Phrenologists try to find out about a personality by
questions.explain: Phrenology (a discredited pseudo-psychology) claimed personality traits could be read from the shape and bumps of a person's skull.

questions.q: The word "psychology" comes from...
questions.explain: Psychology derives from the Greek 'psyche' (soul/mind) and 'logos' (study of).

questions.q: Psychology is an example of
questions.explain: Psychology is conventionally classified as a social science, since it studies the mind and behaviour of individuals within their social context, while also drawing on scientific methodology.

questions.q: The process by which a trained psychologist uses knowledge obtained from psychology to help people solve psychological problems is called...
questions.explain: Psychotherapy is the general term for the practical application of psychological knowledge to help people address psychological problems. Psychoanalysis is one specific type of therapy; psychiatry is a medical specialty.

questions.q: Which of the following is controlled by the thyroid gland?
questions.explain: The thyroid gland produces thyroxine, which regulates the body's metabolic rate.

questions.q: Someone is injured in an accident and he becomes irresponsible and develops impulsive behaviour. Which part of the brain is responsible?
questions.explain: The frontal lobe governs planning, impulse control, and personality regulation — damage here classically produces impulsivity and irresponsibility (as in the famous case of Phineas Gage).

questions.q: Which part of the brain controls reflexes?
questions.explain: Simple reflexes are mediated by reflex arcs at the level of the spinal cord, allowing rapid responses without needing to involve the brain.

questions.q: Who was the father of Experimental Psychology?
questions.explain: Wilhelm Wundt founded the first experimental psychology laboratory in Leipzig, Germany, in 1879, earning him the title 'father of experimental psychology'.

questions.q: J.B. Watson, the founder and father of the behaviouristic school of psychology, defines psychology as the science of ...
questions.explain: Watson founded behaviourism specifically to redefine psychology as the science of observable behaviour, rejecting the study of the unobservable mind or consciousness.

questions.q: Clinical psychology is the practical aspect of
questions.explain: Clinical psychology applies the theory and findings of abnormal psychology to the assessment and treatment of psychological disorders.

questions.q: Psychology is the science and study of
questions.explain: Psychology studies the behaviour and mental processes of living organisms broadly — including both humans and animals — not humans alone.

questions.q: In the __________ method of experiment, passive observation and analysis of human behaviour is usually done.
questions.explain: The observational method involves passively watching and recording behaviour as it naturally occurs, without manipulating any variables.

questions.q: The concept of introspection and conscious experience is associated with...
questions.explain: Structuralism, founded by Wundt and Titchener, used introspection (reporting on one's own conscious experience) to analyse the basic structure of the mind.

questions.q: Self-actualization was proposed by...
questions.explain: Abraham Maslow proposed self-actualization as the pinnacle of his hierarchy of needs — the drive to fulfil one's fullest potential.

questions.q: Psychology at the workplace is...
questions.explain: Industrial and organizational (I/O) psychology is the specialization focused on human behaviour in workplace settings.

questions.q: Height and weight are positively correlated such that
options: As height increases, typically weight increases
Usually the taller one is, the thinner one is
There's no relationship between height and weight
Usually the shorter one is, the heavier the weight
questions.explain: A positive correlation means both variables tend to move in the same direction — as height increases, weight also tends to increase.

questions.q: Too much exercise of the body leads to the risk of harmful diseases. Which type of correlation stipulates the sentence above?
questions.explain: As one variable (amount of exercise) increases, so does the other (risk of harmful disease in this scenario) — both moving in the same direction describes a positive correlation.

questions.q: __________ psychology is associated with emotions, planning, critical thinking and learning.
questions.explain: Cognitive psychology studies mental processes including thinking, planning, learning, and (in applied contexts) their links to emotion.

questions.q: The __________ is the part of the brain associated with fear and aggression.
questions.explain: The amygdala, part of the limbic system, is centrally involved in processing fear and aggressive emotional responses.

questions.q: Which of these is most commonly associated with vision?
questions.explain: The occipital lobe, at the back of the brain, is the primary visual processing centre.

questions.q: A drunk man cannot walk straight because alcohol affects the __________.
questions.explain: The cerebellum controls balance, posture, and coordinated movement — alcohol impairs its function, causing unsteady walking.

questions.q: Which approach to psychology was Edward Titchener associated with in the 1800s?
questions.explain: Edward Titchener brought Wundt's ideas to the US and founded structuralism, focused on analysing the structure of conscious experience.

questions.q: Thorndike's law of effect lies at the heart of which form of learning?
questions.explain: Thorndike's law of effect — that responses followed by satisfying consequences are strengthened — is the foundational principle of operant conditioning.

questions.q: A loud noise startles you and makes you jump. As it occurs several times, you jump less and less each time. This is an example of
questions.explain: A decreasing response to a repeated, harmless stimulus is habituation — a simple, non-associative form of learning.

questions.q: In an experiment testing the effect of temperature on memory, one group sat in a hot room and another in a cold room for 20 minutes, after which both took a memory test. In this study, the independent variable is:
options: The colour of the room's paint
The length of time in the room
questions.explain: The independent variable is the factor the researcher manipulates — here, the room's temperature condition.

questions.q: In the same temperature/memory experiment, the dependent variable is:
options: The room temperature condition (hot vs. cold)
The length of time in the room
The colour of the room's paint
questions.explain: The dependent variable is the outcome being measured — here, how well participants performed on the memory test.

questions.q: In the same temperature/memory experiment, which group is the experimental group?
options: The group placed in the cold room
The group placed in the hot room
questions.explain: The experimental group is the one receiving the condition of interest being tested for its effect — here, the heat manipulation, so the hot room group is the experimental group and the cold room group serves as the control for comparison.

questions.q: In the same temperature/memory experiment, which group is the control group?
options: The group placed in the hot room
The group placed in the cold room
questions.explain: The cold room group serves as the baseline/control against which the effect of heat (on the hot room group) is compared.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT typically a concern of biological psychologists?
questions.explain: Biological psychologists study physiological processes like sleep, thirst, and hunger. Free will is a philosophical concept, not a physiological process, and falls outside biological psychology's typical scope.

questions.q: You are babysitting your little brother, who behaves badly at home. You notice that at a birthday party, he behaves well after seeing other children behave well, and you make a point of rewarding this good behaviour. The method of learning you applied was:
options: Operant conditioning alone, with no observational component
questions.explain: Watching and imitating the other children's good behaviour is observational learning; rewarding that good behaviour to encourage it further is positive reinforcement (itself a principle of operant conditioning) — both mechanisms are at play together.

questions.q: You volunteer for a psychology experiment where the experimenter rings a bell and shoots a puff of air into your eyes, making you blink. After a few trials, you blink as soon as you hear the bell alone. In this example, the bell is the ______, and the puff of air is the ______.
questions.explain: The bell, originally neutral, becomes the conditioned stimulus (CS) once paired with the puff of air. The puff of air naturally and automatically triggers blinking without any learning, making it the unconditioned stimulus (US).

questions.q: In learning, genetic susceptibility:
options: Only affects unlearned reflexes, never learning
Has no effect on learning ability
Can influence a person's learning ability
questions.explain: Individual genetic differences can influence how readily a person learns, alongside environmental and experiential factors.

questions.q: Abena is a medical student who strives to do well in school because she is aware of how hard her father works to pay her tuition. For Abena, obtaining good grades is a __________. questions.q: Which of the following statements about personality and learning is correct?
options: Only intelligence affects learning outcomes, not personality
Learning ability is fixed at birth regardless of personality
Personality can influence how well a person learns
Personality has no bearing on how well a person learns
questions.explain: Personality traits (e.g. conscientiousness, motivation, openness) are well established to influence how effectively a person learns and studies.

questions.q: Which of the following is a recognized principle of operant conditioning?
questions.explain: Extinction — the fading of a behaviour once reinforcement is withheld — is a core principle of operant (and classical) conditioning.

questions.q: "I am primarily interested in thinking processes; I am a __________ psychologist."
questions.explain: Cognitive psychologists specialize in mental processes such as thinking, memory, and problem-solving.

questions.q: Like Carl Rogers, I believe people choose to live more creative and meaningful lives. My name is
questions.explain: Maslow, alongside Rogers, is a founding figure of humanistic psychology, which emphasizes free will and creative, meaningful living.

questions.q: Comparative psychologists are primarily interested in
options: the comparison of different types of psychotherapy.
the comparison of functional and behavioral psychology.
questions.explain: Comparative psychology studies and compares the behaviour of different animal species, often to understand principles applicable to humans.

questions.q: Of the following, who is associated with the Gestalt school of psychology?
questions.explain: Max Wertheimer is a founding figure of Gestalt psychology, famous for studying perceived motion (the phi phenomenon).

questions.q: Of the following, who is a humanistic psychologist?
questions.explain: Abraham Maslow, known for the hierarchy of needs and self-actualization, is a founding humanistic psychologist.

questions.q: Which of the following represents an empirical statement?
options: The temperature today is higher than it was a year ago today.
IQ is defined as mental age, divided by age in years, times 100.
Government experts agree that a future downturn in the economy is likely.
questions.explain: An empirical statement is precisely defined and objectively measurable. The IQ formula is a precise operational definition, unlike the vague or opinion-based other options.

questions.q: A psychologist performs the following experiment: she gives subjects photographs of female faces and asks them to rate the attractiveness of each face. However, some of the subjects have just had to take a very difficult math test, while others have taken a very easy math test. The psychologist would probably be a __________ psychologist.
questions.explain: Studying how a social/emotional state (post-test stress) influences social judgments (attractiveness ratings) falls within social psychology.

questions.q: According to John Watson, introspection was
options: the study of the mind in use.
questions.explain: Watson, the founder of behaviourism, rejected introspection as unscientific because it wasn't objectively observable or measurable.

questions.q: One of the reasons to study psychology is
options: to understand the human mind and how it works.
to completely understand and predict human behavior.
to have the answers to all of life's questions.
to learn how to manipulate others.
questions.explain: A core, legitimate reason to study psychology is to better understand the human mind and how it works — the other options overstate or misrepresent psychology's goals.

questions.q: A psychologist who studies family dynamics and their effects on behavior of individuals in different regions would probably be a __________ psychologist.
questions.explain: Studying how family dynamics vary and affect behaviour across different regions/cultures is the focus of cultural psychology.

questions.q: Which of the following psychological theories is known as the one that emphasizes "free will"?
questions.explain: Humanistic psychology, rooted in existentialist thought, emphasizes free will and personal choice, unlike the deterministic views of psychodynamic and behaviourist theories.

questions.q: The study of similarities and differences in the behavior of different species is called
questions.explain: Comparative psychology specifically studies similarities and differences in behaviour across different animal species.

questions.q: Which of the following is the best example of covert behavior?
options: blinking in response to a light
questions.explain: Covert behaviour is internal and not directly observable by others — remembering something is a private, internal mental event.

questions.q: Which of the following behaviors can best be described as overt behavior?
options: thinking about the answer to a contestant's question
wondering if there are any frozen waffles left in the freezer
being sad that the contestant answered incorrectly
questions.explain: Overt behaviour is directly observable by others. Watching TV is an observable action, unlike the other internal, private mental states listed.

questions.q: Which of the following statements concerning psychodynamic psychology is true?
options: Almost immediately, many of Freud's students broke away from his theories in order to modify and change them.
Freud's theories remain influential today and are largely unchanged from their first conceptualizations.
Freud's theories were very involved and extensive, but they ended up contributing very little to our understanding of human behavior.
Psychodynamic psychology focuses on observable behaviors.
questions.explain: Many of Freud's own students (e.g. Jung, Adler) broke away early on to develop their own modified theories, forming the neo-Freudian movement.

questions.q: Brain mechanisms involved in hunger and thirst would most likely be studied by a
questions.explain: Biopsychologists study the biological/physiological mechanisms (like brain structures) underlying behaviours such as hunger and thirst.

questions.q: "The whole is greater than the sum of its parts" is represented by which of the following?
questions.explain: This is the defining principle of Gestalt psychology — that perception and experience are organized wholes, not just a sum of individual sensory elements.

questions.q: The goals of psychology are to
options: compare, analyze, and control human behavior.
describe, predict, understand, and control behavior.
explain the functioning of the human mind.
questions.explain: The four standard goals of psychology are to describe, explain/understand, predict, and control behaviour.

questions.q: Freud believed that all thoughts and actions are determined by
options: forces in the personality that are often unconscious.
questions.explain: Freud's psychic determinism held that behaviour is driven by often-unconscious forces within the personality (id, ego, superego conflicts).

questions.q: The largest area of specialization among psychologists is
questions.explain: Clinical and counseling psychology represents the largest specialization group among practicing psychologists.

questions.q: The term cognition refers to
questions.explain: Cognition broadly refers to mental processes involved in thinking or knowing — perceiving, reasoning, remembering, and problem-solving.

questions.q: Barbara is applying conditioning principles to teach language skills to retarded children. As a psychologist, her point of view appears to be
questions.explain: Applying conditioning principles to shape behaviour (language skills) is a hallmark of the behaviourist approach.

questions.q: Strict behaviorists were criticized for overlooking the role that __________ plays in our lives.
questions.explain: Strict behaviourism was criticized for ignoring internal cognitive processes like thinking, focusing only on observable stimulus-response behaviour.

questions.q: A psychologist who is "eclectic" can best be described as
options: rejecting determinism in favor of free will.
questions.explain: An eclectic psychologist draws on multiple theoretical approaches rather than adhering strictly to just one school of thought.

questions.q: The study of mental processes such as thinking, perception, information processing, etc. is a key element in __________ psychology.
questions.explain: Cognitive psychology is defined by its focus on mental processes such as thinking, perception, and information processing.

questions.q: Overt behavior is
options: only those things a person does which you can see.
only those things which a person can see with his/her senses.
only those things which can be recorded by a camera.
questions.explain: Overt behaviour specifically refers to actions that are directly observable by others, distinguishing it from private, internal (covert) behaviour.

questions.q: Which area in psychology would be most likely to study the phenomenon of "peer influence"?
questions.explain: Social psychology studies how people are influenced by others, including peer influence and group dynamics.

questions.q: Psychologists are all
questions.explain: Psychologists generally fall into one of two broad roles — researchers/scientists or practitioners — though some do combine both.

questions.q: If you were to walk into a laboratory where the effects of intense punishment on a rat's ability to form a discrimination was being studied, you would be in the lab of a __________ psychologist.
questions.explain: Studying how punishment affects an animal's ability to learn a discrimination task is a classic learning psychology (conditioning) experiment.

questions.q: Maslow proposed a need to develop one's potential and be the best one can be, which he called
questions.explain: Self-actualization is Maslow's term for the need to fulfil one's own unique potential, at the top of his hierarchy of needs.

questions.q: The psychodynamic view emphasizes the role of __________ in development.
questions.explain: The psychodynamic view centers on internal impulses, desires, and unconscious conflicts as the drivers of development and behaviour.

questions.q: Psychology is
options: the scientific study of behavior and mental processes of any living creature.
the study of human origins, evolution, and cultures.
a natural science integrating physiology and neurology.
the deductive study of forms and functions of human groups.
questions.explain: The standard definition of psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes.

questions.q: Of the following, who was a structuralist?
questions.explain: Wundt (along with his student Titchener) is credited with founding structuralism, the school focused on analysing the structure of conscious experience.

questions.q: Some modern psychodynamic theorists, or neo-Freudians, focused on
options: human experience, problems, potentials, and ideals.
social motives and relationships that influence our behavior.
questions.explain: Neo-Freudians (e.g. Adler, Horney) shifted focus toward social motives and relationships as key influences on personality and behaviour.

questions.q: Some topics in psychology are difficult to study because
options: advanced technology that measures brain waves is not available.
of a lack of interest in human behavior.
they overlap with other fields, such as law and business.
questions.explain: Ethical considerations (e.g. the inability to ethically manipulate certain variables in humans) limit what psychologists can directly study.

questions.q: Behaviorism helped make psychology a
questions.explain: By insisting on studying only observable, measurable behaviour, behaviourism helped establish psychology as a rigorous science.

questions.q: Psychiatrists differ from psychologists in that psychiatrists
options: have a Masters or Ph.D. degree with special training in psychological theory and research methods.
are physicians with a specialization in abnormal behavior and psychotherapy.
are generally more eclectic than psychologists.
are extensively trained in the theories and techniques of Sigmund Freud.
questions.explain: Psychiatrists are medical doctors (physicians) who specialize in diagnosing and treating mental disorders, unlike psychologists, who typically are not medical doctors.

questions.q: Developmental psychologists study the effects of __________ on behavior.
questions.explain: Developmental psychology studies how behaviour changes across the lifespan, including the effects of aging.

questions.q: The kind of therapy developed by Freud is called
questions.explain: Freud developed psychoanalysis, a therapy aimed at uncovering unconscious conflicts through techniques like free association.

questions.q: Freud stressed the role of __________ in shaping our personalities.
options: our history of rewards and punishments
questions.explain: Freud placed central importance on the unconscious mind in shaping personality and behaviour.

questions.q: The "father" of psychology and founder of the first psychological laboratory was
questions.explain: Wilhelm Wundt founded the first psychology laboratory in Leipzig in 1879, earning him the title 'father of psychology'.

questions.q: You see a psychologist and tell her that you are feeling depressed. questions.q: The structuralist school of psychology

used introspection to analyze conscious experience.
relied heavily on the concept of natural selection.
questions.explain: Structuralism used introspection — trained self-report of conscious experience — to analyse the basic structure of the mind.

questions.q: "Experience cannot be analyzed successfully into its elements" would likely be said by a
questions.explain: This directly reflects the Gestalt principle that experience must be understood as an organized whole, not broken into separate elements.

questions.q: The key idea in the behavioristic view is that
options: behavior is the result of clashing forces with the personality.
behavior is shaped and controlled by one's environment.
environment plays a very small role in controlling one's behavior.
behavior can be understood in terms of the mental processing of information.
questions.explain: Behaviourism's central idea is that behaviour is shaped and controlled by the environment (through conditioning), not innate/internal forces.

questions.q: Evolutionary psychologists would study
options: developmentally how chimpanzees and humans are similar.
male and female trends in mating choices.
the biological makeup of the human mind across cultures.
historical behavior of a single species.
questions.explain: Evolutionary psychology examines how behaviours have developed over the evolutionary history of a species, shaped by natural selection.

questions.explain: Studying environment-behaviour relationships while disregarding internal experience/consciousness is the definition of behaviourism.

questions.q: The APA professional code stresses
options: cooperation with authorities when a client is suspected of a crime.
deception as a technique to engage the psyche.
use of the scientific method in testing hypotheses.
high levels of competence, integrity, and responsibility.
questions.explain: The American Psychological Association's ethics code emphasizes competence, integrity, and responsibility in professional practice.

questions.q: A psychologist whose viewpoint is psychodynamic
options: believes behavior is directed by forces within one's personality which are often unconscious.
is usually eclectic in his practice.
emphasizes the study of observable behavior.
focuses on self-image and self-actualization to explain behavior.
questions.explain: The psychodynamic viewpoint holds that behaviour is directed by often-unconscious forces within the personality.

This psychologist would probably belong to the __________ school of psychology.
questions.explain: Focusing on personal goals, self-image, and free choice reflects the humanistic school of psychology.

questions.q: A psychologist who studies gender issues focuses on
options: learning the differences between the sexes and how they develop.

questions.q: __________ psychology is concerned with thinking, language, and problem solving.
questions.explain: Cognitive psychology specifically studies thinking, language, and problem-solving processes.

questions.q: Eclectic psychologists are known for
options: stressing the role of the unconscious.
prescribing drugs to treat emotional disorders.
studying the brain and nervous system.
drawing on a variety of theoretical views.
questions.explain: By definition, eclectic psychologists draw on a variety of theoretical perspectives rather than sticking to one school.

questions.q: Psychology is considered a science because it
options: gains information through new methods and technology.
relies on direct observation and measurement of behavior.
studies animal as well as human behavior.
accepts what seems plausible and sensible.
questions.explain: Psychology qualifies as a science because it relies on direct, systematic observation and measurement, not merely plausibility or intuition.

questions.q: Covert behavior is

only those things a person does which you can see.
only those things which are not observable by others.
questions.explain: Covert behaviour refers to private, internal actions/processes that are not observable by others.

questions.q: The proper use of reward, punishment, and behavior modification are results of
questions.explain: Reward, punishment, and behaviour modification techniques are grounded in behaviourist (operant conditioning) principles.

questions.q: The eclectic approach
options: embraces a variety of theoretical views.
has disappeared entirely as a perspective in psychology.
questions.explain: The eclectic approach draws from and embraces multiple theoretical perspectives rather than committing to just one.

questions.q: Repression refers to
options: thoughts mistakenly held out of awareness.
the fact that all thoughts, emotions, and actions are determined.
thoughts actively held out of awareness.
questions.explain: Repression, a Freudian defense mechanism, is the active (though unconscious) exclusion of anxiety-provoking thoughts from awareness.

questions.q: Psychologists use animals in experiments in order to
options: eliminate the effect of the anthropomorphic fallacy.
comply with government prohibitions against any unpleasant experiments using human subjects.
investigate problems that cannot be studied with human subjects in order to discover principles that apply to humans.
questions.explain: Animal research allows investigation of questions that would be unethical or impractical to study directly in humans, aiming to discover broadly applicable principles.

questions.q: A common sense approach to psychology is
options: the basis for collecting data (observed facts).
the basis for most psychological theories.
questions.explain: Common sense beliefs about behaviour are frequently shown to be wrong once tested against rigorous empirical evidence.

questions.q: Of the theorists listed below, who helped to develop the humanistic approach in psychology?
questions.explain: Carl Rogers, alongside Maslow, was a key founder of the humanistic approach to psychology.

questions.q: William James wrote Principles of Psychology and founded

questions.q: Psychodynamic psychology differs from other approaches because it is based on
options: thoughts and impulses outside of conscious experience.

questions.q: The humanistic viewpoint emphasizes
options: the idea that "the environment is the key causal matrix."
determinism, the unconscious, and biological drives.
questions.explain: Humanism centers on free will, self-image, and the drive toward self-actualization.

questions.q: According to John B. Watson, psychology is the study of
questions.explain: Watson redefined psychology as the study of observable behaviour, rejecting the study of the mind/consciousness as unscientific.

questions.q: "I seek to understand the principles whereby a child develops the ability to think, speak, perceive, and learn." This statement identifies one as a __________ psychologist.
questions.explain: Studying how abilities like thinking, speech, and perception develop in children is the focus of developmental psychology.

questions.q: Behavior is
options: only those things which a person can see with his/her senses.
only those things a person does which you can see.
only those things which can be recorded by a camera.
questions.explain: Behaviour broadly refers to anything an organism does, encompassing both overt (observable) and covert (internal) actions.

questions.q: According to the __________ view, the need for love, self-esteem, belonging, self expression, and creativity are as important as biological needs.

questions.q: Biopsychologists
options: are concerned with self-actualization and free will.
attempt to explain behavior in terms of biological or physical mechanisms.
stress the unconscious aspect of behavior.
limit the scope of their study to animals.
questions.explain: Biopsychologists focus on explaining behaviour through biological or physical mechanisms, such as brain function and genetics.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes Maslow's concept of self-actualization?
options: the need to develop one's potential fully
the need to protect one's self-image through self-deception
the need to feel a part of a higher spiritual order
questions.explain: Self-actualization, per Maslow, is the need to fully develop and realize one's own unique potential.
